claims.claim: In Scotland the Key Information Summary is a shared electronic record available across settings, giving clinicians information for people likely to need emergency or out-of-hours care.
claims.supporting_passage: Electronic care coordination systems, known as the Key Information Summary (KIS) in Scotland, enable the creation of shared electronic records available across healthcare settings. A KIS provides clinicians with essential information to guide decision making for people likely to need emergency or out-of-hours care.
claims.pico_timeframe: Scottish primary care; people with advanced progressive illness who died in 2017
claims.safe_wording: In Scotland, the Key Information Summary is a shared record that out-of-hours and emergency clinicians can see, so a plan written there can reach the person who turns up at night.
claims.qualifications: Source says 'available across healthcare settings'; do not list named services beyond that.

claims.claim: Many KIS records lacked key content: 68% included resuscitation status and 55% preferred place of care.
claims.supporting_passage: Overall, 68% (= 482) of KIS included resuscitation status and 55% (= 390) preferred place of care.
claims.pico_timeframe: 712 KIS records of decedents with advanced progressive illness, 18 Scottish practices, deaths in 2017
claims.safe_wording: In one Scottish study of people who died in 2017, about 1 in 3 Key Information Summaries did not record resuscitation status and nearly half did not record preferred place of care.
claims.qualifications: People with advanced progressive illness near death, not all care home or housebound people; 2017 data.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Organ failure patients least likely to have a KIS (47%).

numbers.meaning: 712 of 1034 decedents with advanced progressive illness had a KIS
of KIS recorded preferred place of care

claims.claim: Core hours 08:00-18:30 weekdays total 52.5 of 168 hours, so over two thirds of the week falls outside them.
claims.safe_wording: Say 'most hours of the week fall outside weekday surgery hours' without citing contract hours, or omit.
claims.qualifications: Contract definitions not opened; hours are not demand; England has extended access.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Admission-timing claim and England ReSPECT/shared record claims not sourced; drop them.

claims.claim: Medication errors and unintentional discrepancies after hospital discharge are common.
claims.supporting_passage: For adult patients, the median rate of medication errors and unintentional medication discrepancies following discharge was 53% [interquartile range 33-60.5] (n = 5 studies) and 50% [interquartile range 39-76] (n = 11), respectively.
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults discharged hospital to community; follow-up 2-180 days
claims.safe_wording: Across studies in a systematic review, about half of adults had at least one unintended medicine discrepancy after leaving hospital (median across 11 studies, with wide variation).
claims.qualifications: Medians of few studies; definitions differ; not care-home specific; does not measure the repeat-list mechanism.

numbers.meaning: median unintentional discrepancy rate, 11 studies, patients

claims.claim: Stopped medicines reappear via the GP repeat list and next monthly order; NICE SC1 reconciliation; Discharge Medicines Service; readmission reduction.
claims.safe_wording: Present the repeat-list route as an illustrative example of how a change can be lost, not a measured frequency; do not cite NICE SC1, DMS or readmission effects.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Evaluations of DMS are observational service evaluations.

claims.claim: The INTERACT implementation trial did not show a clear reduction in hospital admissions overall.
claims.supporting_passage: Training and support for INTERACT implementation as carried out in this study had no effect on hospitalization or ED visit rates in the overall population of residents in participating NHs.
claims.pico_timeframe: 85 US nursing homes, 36717 residents; INTERACT training and support vs control; pre-post change
claims.safe_wording: In a US trial across 85 nursing homes, training staff to use the INTERACT tools did not show a clear drop in hospital admissions overall.
claims.qualifications: Potentially avoidable admissions fell but not robust to multiple-comparison correction; do not claim a high-engagement effect.

numbers.meaning: net difference in all-cause hospitalisation, nonsignificant

claims.claim: RESTORE2 (Recognise Early Soft Signs, Take Observations, Respond, Escalate) is used in UK care homes; staff raised training concerns for night and temporary staff.
claims.supporting_passage: there was strong support for using the RESTORE2 (Recognise Early Soft Signs, Take Observations, Respond, Escalate) assessment tool to monitor residents; however, there were concerns about associated training requirements, especially for night and temporary staff.
claims.pico_timeframe: 27 UK care home staff and primary care clinicians, interviews
claims.safe_wording: RESTORE2 (Recognise Early Soft Signs, Take Observations, Respond, Escalate) is a UK care home tool; staff interviewed in one study worried about training night and temporary staff to use it.
claims.qualifications: No effectiveness evidence opened; NEWS2/SBARD components and West Hampshire origin not sourced.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Claim that care workers notice change first was not sourced; frame as judgement.

claims.claim: Covert administration is common and often poorly documented.
claims.supporting_passage: 11% of the patients in regular nursing home units and 17% of the patients in special care units for people with dementia received drugs mixed in their food or beverages at least once during seven days. ... The practice was documented in patients' records in 40% (96/241) of cases.
claims.pico_timeframe: Norwegian nursing home residents, 7-day period, around 2000-2004
claims.safe_wording: In a Norwegian study, about 1 in 9 nursing home residents, and 1 in 6 in dementia units, had medicines hidden in food or drink in one week, and this was written in the record in only 4 in 10 cases.
claims.qualifications: Old Norwegian data; state place and that UK figures may differ.

numbers.meaning: regular units, at least once in 7 days

claims.claim: Tablets with special coatings or modified release, and bitter-tasting medicines, may be unsuitable for crushing or mixing.
claims.supporting_passage: considerations included by consensus in the INGEST algorithm were the presence of special coating or modified release characteristics of the SODF medications, hazardous nature and taste of the active ingredients, manufacturer's advice and use of tube feeding.
claims.safe_wording: Pharmacists check whether a tablet is coated or modified-release, and how it tastes, before it is crushed or mixed into food; ask a pharmacist for each medicine.
claims.qualifications: Expert consensus tool, not harm data.

claims.claim: NICE SC1 and Scottish AWI Act/MWC guide steps (capacity, best interests, section 47 certificate).
claims.safe_wording: Do not attribute specific steps to NICE or MWC; state as professional judgement that hiding medicines should follow a documented capacity and best-interests decision with a pharmacist involved, and reference 'national guidance' without detail only if a later batch opens it.
claims.qualifications: Official documents could not be opened.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: MWC guide may have been updated since 2017.

candidates.reason: Prevalence/documentation (Kirkevold) and crushing principle supported; NICE SC1 and Scottish legal steps not opened.
candidates.revised_angle: Hiding medicines is common and often undocumented (Norwegian data); before a tablet goes in food, ask whether it is still needed and whether a pharmacist has checked it can be crushed or mixed; present documented capacity and best-interests steps as judgement without citing NICE/MWC specifics.

candidates.reason: Post-discharge discrepancy rate supported; repeat-list mechanism, NICE SC1, DMS and readmission claims unsourced.
candidates.revised_angle: About half of adults have an unintended medicine discrepancy after discharge (review median); illustrate one route (repeat list, next order) as an example and name a fix as a recommendation.

candidates.reason: INTERACT trial result and RESTORE2 existence supported; RESTORE2 components/effectiveness and 'care workers notice first' unsourced.
candidates.revised_angle: Centre on the feedback loop as judgement; state the INTERACT trial showed no clear drop in admissions; mention RESTORE2 by name and staff training concerns for night and temporary staff.

candidates.reason: KIS role and content gaps supported by Finucane 2019; contract hours, England routes and admission timing unsourced.
candidates.revised_angle: Write the plan for the out-of-hours reader; in Scotland the KIS carries it, yet in one study a third lacked resuscitation status and nearly half lacked preferred place of care.
